title: Lagrange's Theorem
body:
**For a finite [[Group]] $G$ and any [[Subgroup]] $H \le G$, the order of $H$ divides the order
of $G$:**

$$|G| = [G:H] \cdot |H|$$

The first theorem in the course with real force. It says nothing about which subgroups exist,
but it rules out most sizes before you look, and almost every structural result about finite
groups downstream is a corollary.

## The proof is one sentence of counting

[[Coset]] does the work. The left cosets of $H$ partition $G$, and each has exactly $|H|$
elements. So $|G|$ is the number of blocks times the block size, $[G:H] \cdot |H|$, and $|H|$
divides $|G|$ because it is a factor of it.

That is genuinely the whole argument. What is worth noticing is the shape of it: **build a
partition, count blocks, multiply.** It is the same counting move as [[Combination]] in
[[DISCRETE MATH]], applied to a group instead of a set.

## Consequences, which are the point

- **The order of any element divides $|G|$.** An element $a$ generates a
  [[Cyclic Group|cyclic subgroup]] $\langle a \rangle$ whose size is the order of $a$, and
  Lagrange applies to that subgroup.
- **$a^{|G|} = e$ for every $a \in G$.** The order of $a$ divides $|G|$, so raising to $|G|$
  goes round a whole number of laps.
- **Every group of prime order is cyclic**, and has no subgroups but the two trivial ones. If
  $|G| = p$, any non-identity element generates a subgroup of size dividing $p$ and bigger than
  1, so it generates everything. There is exactly one group of order $p$ up to [[Isomorphism]].
- **Fermat's little theorem**: in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ the non-zero elements form a multiplicative
  group of order $p-1$, so $a^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ whenever $p \nmid a$. Euler's theorem
  $a^{\phi(n)} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ is the same statement for the invertible elements of
  $\mathbb{Z}_n$. **This is how a purely structural theorem turns into the arithmetic that
  [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] runs on**: RSA decryption works because exponents can be reduced modulo
  $\phi(n)$, and that is Lagrange.

## What it does not say

The converse is false. **$d \mid |G|$ does not guarantee a subgroup of order $d$.** $A_4$ has
order 12 and no subgroup of order 6, which is the standard counterexample. Lagrange is a
necessary condition, a filter and not a construction: it tells you where not to look. Partial
converses exist (Cauchy's theorem for prime divisors, the Sylow theorems for prime powers) and
they are the next course's material.

Worked use, which is what an exam asks for:

```
|G| = 15.  What are the possible subgroup orders?
    divisors of 15: 1, 3, 5, 15
    so nothing of order 2, 4, 6, ...
    an element of order 2 is impossible, since <a> would be a subgroup of order 2
```
